passages.3:
When I joined a weekend gardening group, I expected someone to tell me exactly what to do. On my first
morning, however, the organiser, Jo, simply asked what I wanted to learn. I said I knew nothing about
growing food. She gave me a small patch of ground and suggested starting with beans.
For the next month, I watered my plants whenever the surface looked dry. They grew slowly, and I began
to think that gardening wasn't for me. Then another member, Ravi, showed me that the soil underneath
was still wet. I had been giving the plants too much water.
Ravi didn't take over my patch. Instead, he showed me how to check the soil with a finger. Soon the
plants looked healthier. When I finally picked my first beans, there weren't enough for a whole meal, but I
took a photo anyway.
I still ask plenty of questions. Now, though, I understand why Jo didn't give me a long list of instructions.
Making a small mistake, and getting help to understand it, taught me more than following a list would
have done.
passages.4:
For three months, a small customer service company replaced its usual morning meeting with a written
update. Staff posted what they were working on and identified anything that required help. The manager
hoped to recover some of the time that meetings consumed without weakening cooperation.
At first, the change appeared successful. Most employees said that they could begin concentrated work
earlier, and the updates created a searchable record of decisions. Several people who rarely spoke in
meetings contributed detailed suggestions in writing. However, after a few weeks, some newer employees
reported that they were spending longer deciding whom to ask for help. They could read what colleagues
were doing but had fewer opportunities to discover what those colleagues knew.
The company responded by introducing two short, optional question sessions each week. It also asked
experienced staff to add a sentence explaining the reason behind any unfamiliar procedure mentioned in an
update. The amount of written material increased slightly, but repeated questions became less common.
At the end of the trial, the manager resisted describing the change as a simple victory for written
communication. The company had not measured whether customers received better service, and the trial had
taken place during a relatively quiet period. Still, staff wanted to keep the new arrangement.
The experience suggests that replacing meetings is not just a matter of transferring the same information to a
different channel. Meetings may perform several functions at once, including functions nobody notices until
they disappear. A useful redesign begins by identifying those functions, rather than assuming that the most
visible one is the only one that matters.
passages.5:
When the town council invited residents to propose improvements to a public square, it described
the exercise as an opportunity to start with a blank page. This was a generous phrase, though not
an entirely accurate one. The budget had already been fixed, maintenance vehicles needed
access, and a contract required the existing lighting to remain. None of these constraints was
unreasonable. What was questionable was allowing participants to discover them only after
becoming attached to their proposals.
The first workshop produced ambitious designs, followed by predictable disappointment. Some
residents concluded that the council had never intended to listen. Officials, meanwhile, felt unfairly
accused: they had genuinely hoped to receive useful ideas. Both reactions were understandable,
but neither addressed the design of the consultation itself.
For the second workshop, the organisers placed a large map at the entrance, marking what could
change, what could change only at additional cost, and what was fixed. Attendance was lower, yet
the discussion was more specific. Participants disagreed sharply about seating and shade, but
they could explain which trade-offs they preferred. One proposal, initially dismissed as
impractical, was revised into a cheaper version and eventually adopted.
It would be convenient to conclude that transparency automatically creates trust. It does not.
Stating a limit can reveal that the available choice is smaller than people consider acceptable. Nor
does publishing constraints excuse authorities from explaining why those constraints exist. A
boundary presented as technical may still reflect a decision that ought to be open to challenge.
The more modest lesson is that participation needs an honest account of its reach. Inviting people
to influence a decision while concealing where influence ends risks turning enthusiasm into
evidence against the process. A useful consultation need not promise that every proposal can
succeed. It should enable participants to distinguish between an idea rejected on its merits and an
idea that was never eligible for consideration. Without that distinction, even a sincerely offered
invitation can sound, afterwards, like a performance.
passages.6:
At the opening of our neighbourhood's repaired footbridge, the speeches dwelt on speed. The
project, we were told, had been completed in fourteen weeks. This was true in the carefully
delimited sense that fourteen weeks had passed between the arrival of the builders and the
removal of the barriers. The years during which residents had requested a repair belonged,
apparently, to another clock.
It is tempting to dismiss this as ordinary publicity, and perhaps that would be fair. An opening
ceremony is not an audit. Yet the choice of when a story begins does more than flatter the people
telling it. It determines which forms of effort become visible. In this version, the bridge emerged
from a decisive intervention; the patient work of reporting damage, gathering signatures and
attending meetings was merely the weather in which the intervention occurred.
A neighbour suggested adding a plaque thanking the campaigners. I liked the proposal, although I
doubted that a longer list of names would resolve the problem. Recognition can be extended while
the underlying account remains intact: the public asks, the institution acts, and gratitude flows in
the expected direction. What disappears is the possibility that repeatedly having to ask was itself
part of the failure.
This does not mean that the engineers deserve less credit. Their achievement is no smaller
because it sits within a less comfortable story. Indeed, treating criticism of the process as criticism
of the repair makes it unnecessarily difficult to appreciate either accurately. We should be able to
admire the bridge and still inquire why its necessity took so long to become an official fact.
The bridge is now busy, which is the strongest argument for having repaired it and no answer at
all to the question of delay. People crossing with shopping bags are not obliged to carry a history
lesson as well. Institutions, however, have a different responsibility. If they measure success only
from the moment they authorise action, they may learn to become impressively efficient at solving
problems they have spent years declining to recognise.
Perhaps the next opening speech could give two dates: when work began, and when the need
was first accepted as credible by those who lived with it. The resulting story would be less tidy. It
might also make the next repair happen sooner, which seems a more useful tribute to this one
than another adjective about speed.
